A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sparsity Forcing with the same authors and core framework. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v2 ends with references; v4 additionally contains Appendix A.1–A.5.

before.justification: v2 reports original image/video benchmark evaluations, runtime measurements, ablations, and robustness results in Tables 1–5 and Figures 3–6.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds reward-design experiments, training-cost measurements, a temperature baseline, and failure cases.

M1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds an evaluated variant incorporating measured latency into the efficiency reward; the core GRPO and default reward equations remain unchanged. The new full-cache, decoding-only selection statement in Section 3.2 conflicts with Section 3.1 and Algorithm 1, so an actual replacement of the default caching procedure cannot be established.

E1.justification: Training datasets, thirteen main benchmarks, and HallusionBench are retained. Figure 7 adds two explicitly tested video spatial-estimation scenarios involving object distance and room area, providing a limited diagnostic extension. Their dataset provenance is unspecified.

E2.justification: Table 8 adds an attention-temperature adjustment baseline to the post-training accuracy comparison. Table 7 also introduces a cost comparison involving MOBA, post-trained ZipVL, and sharpness loss. Comparator membership in the retained main accuracy tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: v4 adds a controlled comparison of efficiency-reward variants and a training-time/latency comparison with latency measured at a 128k context. Existing model configurations, frame counts, and main training/inference thresholds remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 newly documents settings for existing ablations rather than establishing revised settings.

E4.justification: Appendices A.4–A.5 add two spatial-reasoning failure cases, an ablation testing whether latency improves the efficiency reward, and training/rollout cost analysis. Existing pruning-strategy, budget/group-size, attention-distribution, scaling, and HallusionBench analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seed replication, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. GRPO rollout groups and within-group reward standardization remain unchanged and are not uncertainty estimates for benchmark results.

E6.justification: Table 3 changes averages despite unchanged component scores: Full changes from 70.2 to 73.2 and Sparsity Forcing from 70.0 to 72.8. Tables 6–8 add reward-variant, cost, and temperature-baseline results; Figure 7 adds spatial-estimation failures. The latency-reward variant reports 61.2 average accuracy at 30.5% tokens versus 61.3 at 29.6% for the retained variant. Table 8 repeats old averages inconsistent with revised Table 3; main benchmark scores otherwise remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly supplies mathematical definitions for pooled-query/key attention and the negative mean rowwise L-infinity sharpness loss, previously described verbally. This formalizes an existing baseline. Equations (1)–(11), the cited approximation bound, and existing assumptions remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion retain the same RL-based sparsity framework and headline claims: thirteen benchmarks, token reduction increasing from approximately 20% to 75%, up to threefold memory reduction, and up to 3.3-fold speedup.

C2.justification: v4 adds an explanation linking spatial failures to disrupted cross-frame correspondences, interprets token reduction as a sufficient hardware-efficiency surrogate, and argues that additional training cost is worthwhile. The conclusion replaces v2's specific sequential-rollout/batching limitation with single-turn, hardware-agnostic scope and multi-turn future work, without demonstrating that batching was resolved.

D1.justification: Appendices A.1–A.3 substantially expand implementation documentation with prefill/decoding pseudocode, attention-probing and sharpness-loss details, and training/inference settings for top-k and threshold pruning. Section 4 newly reports 883 and 164 GPU-hours for Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-Video-7B. These are disclosures rather than evidence of reruns; the conflicting full-cache statement limits reproducibility.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations to PagedAttention for cache access and ZipCache for attention-score normalization. Existing related-work coverage and positioning against training-free pruning, trainable sparse attention, and sharpness regularization remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section ordering are retained. Changes include limited grammatical edits, an equal-contribution note, a revised limitations paragraph, and a five-part appendix organizing implementation details and additional analyses.

P2.justification: v4 adds two algorithm panels, an annotated video failure-case figure, and Tables 6–8; Table 8 extends and redisplays the earlier post-training comparison. Main results pages are substantially repacked through relocation of Tables 2–5 and resizing of plots. Figures 1–6 retain their underlying visual content.

improvement.justification: v4 provides useful implementation detail, cost measurements, reward controls, and concrete failure diagnostics absent from v2. However, its new full-cache statement contradicts the retained pruning description and Algorithm 1, leaving a central efficiency mechanism unresolved. Tables 3 and 8 also report incompatible averages for identical component scores, weakening the added baseline interpretation. These documentation gains and material consistency problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
